lessons.title: Linked List Structure
lessons.concept: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are stored non-contiguously. Each node typically contains data and a reference/pointer to the next node. The list is accessed via a head pointer to the first node; the last node points to null/None.
lessons.formula: Node = {data, next}. Traversal: start at head, follow next pointers until null.
lessons.worked_example: List: [10] -> [20] -> [30] -> null. Head points to node with 10. To reach 30, follow head->next->next.
mistakes: Confusing linked list nodes with array indices (no direct random access)
Forgetting to update the head when inserting/deleting at the beginning
Losing references and causing unintended list breaks

lessons.title: Basic Linked List Operations
lessons.concept: Common operations include traversal, insertion (at beginning, end, or position), deletion, and search. Insertion/deletion at a known node can be O(1) if pointer is known, but finding a position usually requires traversal (O(n)).
lessons.formula: Traversal/Search: O(n). Insert/delete at head: O(1). Insert/delete after given node: O(1) (excluding search time).
lessons.worked_example: Insert 5 at beginning of [10]->[20]: create node(5), set 5.next = head, update head to node(5). Result: [5]->[10]->[20].
mistakes: Not handling empty list or single-element cases
Updating pointers in wrong order during insertion/deletion
Assuming O(1) access by index like arrays

lessons.title: Types and Trade-offs
lessons.concept: Singly linked lists have next pointers only. Doubly linked lists have next and previous pointers, enabling bidirectional traversal but using extra memory. Circular linked lists connect the last node back to the first. Linked lists offer efficient insert/delete at known positions but poor cache locality and no constant-time indexing compared to arrays.
lessons.formula: Singly: next. Doubly: prev + next. Circular: tail.next points to head (or forms a cycle).
lessons.worked_example: In a doubly linked list [A]<->[B]<->[C], from B you can move to A via prev and to C via next without restarting from head.
mistakes: Confusing singly and doubly linked list pointer requirements
Ignoring extra memory overhead of doubly linked lists
Assuming linked lists are always better than arrays for all operations

practice.question: In a singly linked list, what does each node typically store (besides data)?
practice.explanation: A singly linked list node stores its data and a reference/pointer to the next node in the sequence.

practice.question: What is the time complexity to access the k-th element in a singly linked list (by traversal from head)?
practice.explanation: Linked lists do not support direct indexing; reaching the k-th element requires traversing nodes from the head, which is O(n) in the worst case.

practice.question: Inserting a new node at the beginning of a singly linked list (given head pointer) has what time complexity?
practice.explanation: Insertion at head requires creating a node and updating a couple of pointers (new node's next and head), which takes constant time O(1).

practice.question: Which linked list type allows traversal in both forward and backward directions?
practice.explanation: A doubly linked list stores both next and previous pointers in each node, allowing traversal in both directions.

options.C: Better cache locality in all cases

questions.explanation: Linked lists can insert/delete nodes by updating pointers without shifting contiguous elements. However, they lack O(1) indexing and have pointer overhead.

questions.explanation: In an unsorted linked list, you may need to check each node sequentially until found or end is reached, which is O(n) in the worst case.

questions.question: In a circular linked list, which statement is true?

options.A: The last node points to null
options.B: The last node points back to the first node (or head)

questions.explanation: A circular linked list forms a cycle by having the last node's next reference point to the first/head node instead of null.

options.B: A pointer to the previous node
options.C: A pointer to the middle node

questions.question: If the head pointer of a non-empty singly linked list is lost and no other references exist, what happens to the list nodes (in typical managed/unmanaged contexts)?

options.A: They become the first element of an array automatically
options.B: They are still directly accessible by index
options.C: The list becomes inaccessible (and may be garbage collected/leaked depending on environment)
options.D: The last node becomes the new head automatically

questions.explanation: The head pointer is the entry point to traverse a singly linked list. Losing it without other references makes the nodes unreachable/inaccessible.
